summary: Specifies the Versatile Message Transaction Protocol (VMTP), a transport protocol designed for the request-and-response style of communication used by remote procedure calls. It offers features such as security, real-time use, streaming, multicast and idempotency, and can be trimmed down for simple clients and servers. It was experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: Most talks online are ask-and-answer. VMTP is a messenger designed for that: send a question, get a reply, with extras you can switch on or leave off.

subtitle: A request-response transport protocol built for RPC and file access, with its own names, multicast, security and streaming.

tldr.problem: TCP needs extra packets for isolated request-response calls, is hard to implement, handles packet overruns poorly, names endpoints by host address and port, and offers no multicast, real-time datagrams or security.
tldr.mechanism: VMTP sends a request message to a server or group of servers and gets back zero or more responses, with no separate connection setup. Endpoints have 64-bit host-independent identifiers, and messages travel as packet groups with selective retransmission and rate-based flow control.
tldr.outcome: The memo is labelled Experimental. It describes a design still being implemented in the UNIX 4.3BSD and V kernels, and it leaves open questions such as the size and algorithm of the checksum.

today: RFC 1045 is labelled Experimental, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes version 0.7 of the protocol and was still being implemented and refined when published.

sections.title: Why a New Transport Protocol
sections.content:
The Versatile Message Transaction Protocol (VMTP) is a transport protocol for remote procedure call (RPC) and other transaction-oriented traffic. In a transaction, a client sends a request, the server processes it and replies, and there are no separate operations to set up or tear down an association. The server may throw away its state about a client between transactions without causing failures.

The RFC compares VMTP with TCP and names three weaknesses it wants to fix. First, RPC performance: TCP needs extra packets for connection setup and clearing, is hard to implement, and handles packet loss from overruns poorly. Second, naming: a TCP endpoint is an Internet address plus a port, so it is tied to one host interface, which causes trouble for process migration, mobile hosts and multi-homed hosts. Third, missing functions: TCP has no multicast, real-time datagrams or security.

VMTP is designed to run on a simple unreliable datagram service such as IP. It can also run directly on network or data link layers when internetwork services are not needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking a quick question over TCP is like having to phone someone, say hello, ask, and say goodbye. VMTP lets you just send the question and get the answer.

sections.title: Entities, Domains and Message Transactions
sections.content:
VMTP talks between network-visible entities, which usually stand for a message port or a procedure invocation. Entity, process and principal identifiers are each 64 bits long, but only entity identifiers are actively used by the protocol. An entity identifier must be unique, stable (it does not change meaning without staying invalid for at least a time T) and independent of the host address, so an entity can migrate or sit on a mobile or multi-homed host.

A set of entities can form an entity group with one identifier. An entity domain is the administration that guarantees uniqueness and stability for its identifiers, and only entities in the same domain communicate directly via VMTP.

A message transaction is a request message from the client followed by zero or more responses, at most one per server entity. Within a domain a transaction is identified by the client, a 32-bit Transaction number and a 4-bit ForwardCount. Each message has a message control block plus segment data, with a maximum message size of 4 megaoctets.
sections.plainLanguage: Every talker gets a name tag that stays the same even if they change buildings. A question goes out, and answers come back with the same question number on them.

sections.title: Packet Groups and Reliability
sections.content:
A message is sent as one or more packet groups. A packet group is up to 32 packets sent as a single blast with no explicit flow control, covering up to 16 kilooctets of segment data. A PacketDelivery bit mask says which 512-octet blocks each packet carries, so the receiver can ask for just the missing pieces. The RFC requires the underlying datagram service to carry at least the basic 580 octet VMTP packet.

Reliability comes from transaction identifiers (used to drop duplicate requests), a checksum, positive acknowledgments and timeouts with retransmission. Each packet has a 32-bit checksum, and a zero checksum field means none was sent. The RFC suggests 5 retries for requests and responses. Acknowledgments and retransmission requests travel as notify operations to the peer's management module.

For flow control, the client estimates an interpacket gap, expressed in 1/32nds of the MTU packet transmission time, with a maximum of 8 packet times. Selective retransmission means that pushing against the maximum rate costs little, since only the dropped packets are resent.
sections.plainLanguage: A big parcel is split into numbered boxes. If a few boxes go missing, the receiver says which ones, and only those are sent again.

sections.title: Multicast, Real-Time, Streaming and Forwarding
sections.content:
If the server identifier names an entity group, the request is multicast to every entity in the group on a best-efforts basis, and the client may receive multiple responses. A coresident-entity field lets a request reach the subgroup of servers on the same host as a given entity.

For real-time use, each message carries a priority, datagram requests need no response or retransmission, and flags give conditional delivery (CMD), header-only checksums (HCO) and no retransmission (NRT). Idempotent responses are not stored: the request is simply redone if the response is lost.

Streaming lets a client start further transactions before the first response arrives. They form a run with consecutive transaction identifiers, which act as sequence numbers. A server can also forward a request so that another server answers the client directly, up to a maximum forward count of 15. Streaming and the fault-tolerance receive-sequence support are described as optional or experimental.
sections.plainLanguage: You can shout a question to a whole room, ask many questions without waiting for each answer, or hand your question to a friend who answers you directly.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
VMTP has an optional secure mode meant to stop peeking, impostoring, message tampering and replays. The RFC says non-secure VMTP gives no guarantees against an intelligent intruder who can change packets and update the checksum.

Secure packets are flagged with the EPG bit and are encrypted with a working key shared by client and server, except for the Client, Version, Domain, Length and Packet Flags fields. Key and identity information is obtained through an authenticated Probe operation. Replays and impostors are caught by checking the Transaction identifier, and tampering is caught because an intruder cannot fix the checksum without the key. A separate key distribution and authentication protocol is needed, and multiple authentication domains allow different encryption algorithms.
sections.plainLanguage: Secure mode puts the message in a locked box that only the right receiver has the key to. Anyone who changes the box cannot hide that they did.

sections.title: Minimal Implementations and Experience
sections.content:
VMTP is built so simple devices can use a subset. A minimal client sends a request packet group, receives a response and answers management requests such as Probe. A minimal server handles idempotent, unencrypted transactions and may need no timers or buffering, which suits a network boot loader, time server, sensor or actuator. Over IP, VMTP uses protocol number 81, and hosts agree to accept VMTP/IP packets of at least 600 octets.

The RFC reports partial implementations (without streaming and full security) in the V kernel and the 4.3 BSD Unix kernel. In the V kernel a transaction with no data between two Sun-3/75s on 10 Mb Ethernet took 2.25 milliseconds. The concluding remarks say these are experimental implementations and that the checksum size and algorithm were still under discussion.
sections.plainLanguage: Simple gadgets can use a tiny version of the rules, like a toy with only two buttons, while bigger computers use the full set.
